intro: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. Only a handful have been imaged directly; the rest are known from the orbits of the stars around them, from the X-rays of gas falling in, or from the gravitational waves released when two of them merge. Masses are given in solar masses (M☉) and the diameter quoted is that of the event horizon.

classes.name: Stellar-mass
classes.description: Left behind when a massive star collapses at the end of its life. Most are found because they pull gas from a companion star, which glows in X-rays as it falls in.

classes.name: Intermediate-mass
classes.description: The rarest and least understood class, sitting between collapsed stars and the giants in galactic centres. Candidates are found in dense star clusters and in unusually bright X-ray sources.

classes.name: Supermassive
classes.description: Millions to tens of billions of solar masses, sitting at the centre of nearly every large galaxy. When they feed they light up as quasars, the brightest sustained sources in the universe.

blackHoles.name: Sagittarius A*
blackHoles.discovery: Radio source found in 1974; imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2022
blackHoles.summary: The black hole at the centre of our own galaxy. Decades of tracking the orbits of stars around it — work that won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics — pinned down its mass long before the Event Horizon Telescope produced its picture of the glowing ring of gas around its shadow.

image.alt: Orange ring of glowing gas surrounding the dark shadow of the black hole Sagittarius A*.

blackHoles.name: M87*
blackHoles.discovery: Jet noted in 1918; first black hole ever imaged, in 2019
blackHoles.summary: The first black hole to be photographed. The Event Horizon Telescope combined radio dishes across the planet into an Earth-sized instrument to resolve the shadow at the heart of the giant elliptical galaxy M87, which also drives a jet of plasma 5,000 light-years long.

image.file: Black hole - Messier 87 crop max res.jpg
image.alt: The first image of a black hole: a bright orange ring of light around the dark shadow of M87*.

blackHoles.name: TON 618
blackHoles.galaxy: Host galaxy of the quasar TON 618
blackHoles.discovery: Catalogued in 1957; recognised as a quasar in 1970
blackHoles.summary: One of the most massive black holes known. Its event horizon would swallow the entire Solar System many times over, and the quasar it powers outshines its host galaxy so completely that the galaxy itself has never been seen.

image.alt: Artist's impression of a quasar: a brilliant disc of hot gas spiralling into a distant supermassive black hole.

blackHoles.name: Phoenix A
blackHoles.designation: Central black hole of the Phoenix Cluster
blackHoles.discovery: Cluster identified in 2010 by the South Pole Telescope
blackHoles.summary: The black hole at the centre of the Phoenix Cluster is among the largest ever estimated. The cluster around it forms stars at a furious rate — hundreds of solar masses a year — because the cooling gas at its core is not fully held back by the black hole's outbursts.

image.alt: X-ray and optical composite of the Phoenix Cluster, a bright galaxy cluster with a cooling core.

blackHoles.name: P2 (Andromeda's core)
blackHoles.discovery: Double nucleus resolved by the Hubble Space Telescope in 1993
blackHoles.summary: The black hole in our nearest large neighbour sits inside a curious double nucleus: a lopsided disc of old red stars orbits it, so from Earth the core of Andromeda appears to have two peaks of light.

image.alt: The Andromeda Galaxy, a bright spiral seen at an angle, whose core hosts a supermassive black hole.

blackHoles.name: Centaurus A's engine
blackHoles.discovery: Radio galaxy identified in 1949; black hole mass measured from 1999
blackHoles.summary: The nearest active galactic nucleus. Gas funnelling into the black hole launches radio jets a million light-years long, which the Event Horizon Telescope resolved in 2021 right down to the point where they are launched.

image.alt: Centaurus A, an elliptical galaxy crossed by a thick dark dust lane, powered by a central black hole.

blackHoles.name: Cygnus X-1
blackHoles.discovery: X-ray source found in 1964; accepted as a black hole in the 1970s
blackHoles.summary: The first object widely accepted as a black hole, and the subject of a famous bet between Stephen Hawking and Kip Thorne. It pulls a stream of gas from a blue supergiant companion; the gas heats to millions of degrees as it spirals in and shines in X-rays.

image.alt: Artist's impression of Cygnus X-1 drawing a stream of gas from its blue supergiant companion star.

blackHoles.name: V404 Cygni
blackHoles.discovery: Nova recorded in 1938; identified as a black hole binary in 1989
blackHoles.summary: A black hole that spends decades quiet and then erupts. Its 2015 outburst made it briefly one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky and let astronomers watch a wobbling, warped accretion disc in real time.

image.alt: Artist's impression of the black hole V404 Cygni pulling material from its companion star into a bright accretion disc.

blackHoles.name: A0620−00
blackHoles.discovery: X-ray nova of 1975; mass measured in 1986
blackHoles.summary: One of the closest known black holes to Earth and the second object to be confirmed as one. Today it is dormant, and its orange dwarf companion circles it every 7.75 hours.

image.file: Black hole with accretion disk and jet.jpg
image.alt: Illustration of a stellar-mass black hole surrounded by a hot accretion disc of gas drawn from a companion star.

blackHoles.name: Gaia BH1
blackHoles.summary: The nearest known black hole. It is dark and quiet — no gas is falling in — and was found purely from the wobble it imposes on a Sun-like star that orbits it every 186 days.

image.file: Artist's impression of a black hole and its companion star.jpg
image.alt: Artist's impression of a quiet, dormant black hole orbited by a Sun-like companion star.

blackHoles.name: Gaia BH3
blackHoles.summary: The most massive stellar black hole known in our galaxy, and the second closest. Its companion is an ancient, metal-poor giant star, which suggests the black hole formed from one of the first generations of massive stars.

image.file: Artist's impression of the Gaia BH3 system.jpg
image.alt: Artist's impression of the Gaia BH3 system, a massive dormant black hole orbited by an old giant star.

blackHoles.name: GW150914 remnant
blackHoles.summary: Not seen but heard: two black holes spiralled together and radiated three solar masses of energy as ripples in spacetime. The signal lasted a fifth of a second, confirmed a century-old prediction of general relativity and opened gravitational-wave astronomy.

image.alt: The LIGO gravitational-wave signal of GW150914, showing the rising chirp of two merging black holes.

blackHoles.name: M82 X-1
blackHoles.discovery: Identified as an intermediate-mass candidate in 2014
blackHoles.summary: The brightest X-ray source in the starburst galaxy M82, far too luminous for an ordinary stellar black hole. The rhythm of its X-ray flickering points to a black hole of a few hundred solar masses — one of the best intermediate-mass candidates.

image.alt: The Cigar Galaxy M82, an edge-on starburst galaxy venting red filaments of glowing hydrogen.
image.credit: NASA, ESA and the Hubble Heritage Team

blackHoles.name: HLX-1
blackHoles.summary: A hyper-luminous X-ray source sitting off to one side of the galaxy ESO 243-49, probably the stripped core of a small galaxy that was swallowed. It remains the strongest case for an intermediate-mass black hole.

image.alt: Hubble image of the galaxy ESO 243-49 with the intermediate-mass black hole candidate HLX-1 marked at its edge.

blackHoles.name: Omega Centauri's core
blackHoles.summary: Seven stars racing through the centre of the largest globular cluster in the Milky Way move too fast to be held by the cluster's stars alone. The simplest explanation is an intermediate-mass black hole hiding in the crowd.

image.alt: The globular cluster Omega Centauri, a dense ball of millions of stars, imaged from Chile.
